newsitem.title: TAIWAN: As world crude eases, Taiwan raises oil prices.
newsitem.headline: As world crude eases, Taiwan raises oil prices.

text.p: Taiwan state monopoly Chinese Petroleum said on Friday it was raising oil prices for a second time in three months, citing unexpectedly high crude costs despite a major fall in world prices.
The company said the average 2.97 percent hike, effective from 0001 on April 5 (1601 GMT April 4), was needed to trim chronic budget shortfalls.
The increase is the second in three months, following an average nine percent on January 1 rise that the oil monopoly also blamed on unexpectedly high crude import costs.
In a statement, the company said its crude import costs in March had risen to US$20.26 a barrel compared to just US$16.75 in January, far higher than forecasters had budgeted for.
"We need to make some adjustment to reflect import costs in the remaining three months (of the July-June fiscal year)," the statement said.

Because of a national holiday on Friday, Chinese Petroleum officials could not be reached for comment on why Taiwan's crude import costs had risen some 21 percent just as world crude prices were tumbling by an even greater percentage.
Brent crude futures, a world benchmark, hit US$24.57 per barrel on January 9 but were just US$18.18 at the close of trading in London on Thursday -- a decline of 26 percent.
The increase had been authorised in principle in December.

After months of debate, the economic ministry on December 31 approved an overall 12 percent hike but ordered it staggered between January and April for fear of fanning inflation just as a sluggish economic recovery seemed to be gaining steam.
Company spokesman Tsai Shan-lang, speaking briefly on state television, said the increase needed no state authorisation as it fell within a monthly adjustment limit of three percent.
At the time of the first increase, Chinese Petroleum said it would need an aggregate increase of 14 percent to break even.
It said on Friday it had accumulated a T$1.965 billion (US$71.5 million) deficit between July and February.
In February alone, the company posted a pre-tax loss of T$486 million, compared with a targeted pre-tax profit of T$1.538 billion.
Almost totally dependent on foreign crude, Taiwan imports more than 150 million barrels a year.
At the gas pump, the retail price of 92-octane and 95-octane petrol would rise 40 cents per litre (5.5 U.S. cents per gallon) to T$17.1 and T$18.1 respectively on April 5, it said.
It was unclear how the latest increase would affect Taiwan's consumer prices, but company officials told state radio they did not expect a major inflationary impact.
The central bank vowed to closely monitor related consumer prices, state radio said.
Consumer prices rose 2.03 percent year-on-year in February.
The company said the increase had nothing to do with a spate of serious fires, oil spills and explosions that plagued the company in 1996, triggering huge compensation claims.
"The T$870 million accident compensation has been absorbed by the company through the team effort of reducing operating costs and increasing productivity," it said.
"The compensation is not in any way reflected in the price adjustment," the company statement added.
Industry sources nonetheless have blamed the company's huge deficit in part to inefficient management.

Although parliament enacted laws in 1996 dismantling Chinese Petroleum's monopoly, Taiwan's sole producer will not face competition before 1999 when a refinery being built by giant would-be rival Formosa Plastics goes on line.
